extraReferences.title: Himantolophus. Footballfishes. Tree of Life Web Project
Family Himantolophidae: Footballfishes, Prickly Deepsea Anglerfishes

anatomy.lede: The female footballfish is a round, spiny body with a vast mouth and a glowing rod on its head. This preserved specimen shows her lure, but not its light.

hotspots.label: Fishing rod
hotspots.text: The rod, or illicium, is a modified fin spine. In this species it measures 28–54% of the body length.

hotspots.label: Lure
hotspots.text: The bulb at the tip, the esca, holds glowing bacteria. Its size and shape vary more than in other deep-sea anglerfishes.

hotspots.label: Lure appendages
hotspots.text: Branched and unbranched tentacle-like appendages sprout from the bulb, with light-guiding appendages at its tip.

hotspots.label: Tiny eye
hotspots.text: Females have small to tiny eyes, unlike the well-developed eyes of the males.

hotspots.label: Mouth
hotspots.text: The large, slanting mouth has a stout lower jaw that juts beyond the upper, lined with slender, curved teeth that fold inwards.

hotspots.label: Skin spines
hotspots.text: Large conical spines are scattered over the head and body. The bumps are the bases of these spines, which may put off predators.

hotspots.label: Pectoral fin
hotspots.text: Footballfishes have no pelvic fins at all. The short dorsal and anal fins sit far back, near the tail.

senses.lede: Males and females are built for different jobs. Females wait in the dark; males must search it for a mate.

senses.name: A male's nose
senses.text: Males have large smelling organs with nostrils facing sideways, and are thought to find females by smell.

senses.name: A male's eyes
senses.text: Males have well-developed eyes, 5.5–8.7% of their body length across, and directed to the sides.

senses.name: A female's eyes
senses.text: Females have small to tiny eyes; instead of searching for food, they lure it to them.

body.lede: Everything about the female is designed to bring food to her mouth and keep it there.

systems.title: Borrowed light
systems.text: The lure does not make its own light. It glows because of living light-producing bacteria, Photobacterium, housed inside it.

systems.title: A fluorescent lure?
systems.text: In a Pacific footballfish, the lure also showed fluorescence, the first recorded in a deep-sea anglerfish. Whether this helps attract prey or mates is unknown.

systems.title: Gripping without teeth
systems.text: Males have no jaw teeth. Instead, bony plates on the snout and chin carry 16–31 and 20–50 hooked denticles, used to grip a female temporarily.

survival.lede: Footballfishes are rarely seen alive; most of what is known comes from specimens caught in nets or found inside whales.

tactics.title: A trap of teeth
tactics.text: Prey is whatever fits into the mouth, and backward-curving teeth stop it escaping.

tactics.title: Spiny skin
tactics.text: The spines scattered over the body may deter predators.

life.lede: Footballfishes start as tiny, round larvae near the surface and change shape completely before descending.

stages.name: Egg and larva
stages.text: Eggs and larvae drift in open water. The larvae are short and almost spherical, with puffed-up skin, and reach 17–22.5 mm.

stages.name: Metamorphosis
stages.text: Even as larvae, females can be told apart by a small club-shaped stub of the future rod on the head. Larvae transform into their adult shape at about 20–33 mm.

stages.name: Free-living male
stages.text: Males are free-living and never parasitic. They are thought to cling to a female only briefly, though no male has yet been found attached to one.

stages.name: Female
stages.text: Females keep growing long after the males stop. The largest known female of this species, from south-west Greenland, measured about 46.5 cm in standard length; some sources give up to about 60 cm.
